introduction-the-language-of-the-web.core: HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol. A client sends a method, a path, headers and an optional body; the server returns a status code, headers and an optional body. Statelessness means every request carries everything needed to process it (cookies, tokens), which lets any server behind a load balancer handle it. That property is what makes the web horizontally scalable.

first_principles.problem: A team stores session state in server memory, and users get logged out whenever the load balancer switches servers.
truths: Context must travel with the request.
Any server can serve stateless requests.

analogy.title: Ordering at a counter with a ticket
analogy.story: Each order slip contains everything needed; any cook can prepare it without remembering you.
analogy.breaks: Cooks may remember regulars; servers shouldn't rely on memory.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Token carries identity; any server can answer.

code.text:
GET /api/orders/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0

{"id":42,"status":"shipped"}

check.q: Why does HTTP statelessness help scaling?
check.a: Any server can handle any request because no per-client memory is needed, so you can add servers behind a load balancer freely.

http-verbs-the-actions.core: Methods express intent. GET reads, POST creates or triggers processing, PUT replaces a resource at a known URL, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes, HEAD fetches headers only, and OPTIONS describes capabilities (and handles CORS preflight). Using them correctly lets caches, proxies, retries and API tooling behave safely; tunnelling everything through POST throws that away.

first_principles.problem: An API uses GET /deleteUser?id=5, and a link prefetcher deletes users.
truths: Correct verbs enable caching and retries.

analogy.title: Library actions
analogy.story: Reading a book (GET), donating a new one (POST), replacing a copy (PUT), correcting a page (PATCH), removing it (DELETE).
analogy.breaks: Librarians notice misuse; crawlers and caches don't.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Clients, caches and retries know what's safe.

code.text:
GET    /orders          list
POST   /orders          create → 201 Location: /orders/42
GET    /orders/42       read
PUT    /orders/42       replace
PATCH  /orders/42       {"status":"cancelled"}
DELETE /orders/42       → 204

check.q: Why is a state-changing GET dangerous?
check.a: Crawlers, prefetchers, caches and retries assume GET is safe and may trigger it without user intent.

status-codes-the-feedback.core: Status codes come in classes. 1xx is informational, 2xx success (200, 201, 204), 3xx redirection (301 permanent, 302/307 temporary, 304 not modified), 4xx client errors (400, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404, 409, 429 rate limited), and 5xx server errors (500, 502 bad gateway, 503 unavailable, 504 gateway timeout). Codes drive client retries, caching, monitoring and SLOs.

first_principles.problem: An API returns 200 with {"error":"failed"}, so monitoring shows 100% success during an outage.
truths: Machines act on codes, not bodies.
derivation: **4xx** for client mistakes; **5xx** for server faults.

analogy.title: Traffic lights for clients
analogy.story: Green (2xx) go, yellow (3xx) go elsewhere, red (4xx) you did something wrong, flashing red (5xx) the road itself is broken.
analogy.breaks: Traffic lights have three states; HTTP has dozens of nuanced codes.

example.title: Proxy errors decoded
flow: 502: LB got bad/no response from upstream
example.outcome: meaningful feedback for clients and monitors.

check.a: 401 means not authenticated (credentials missing/invalid); 403 means authenticated but not allowed.

headers-the-metadata.core: Headers carry everything that isn't the body. Request headers carry routing (Host), negotiation (Accept, Accept-Encoding), auth (Authorization, Cookie) and context (User-Agent, X-Forwarded-For, traceparent). Response headers carry content metadata (Content-Type, Content-Length), caching (Cache-Control, ETag, Vary), cookies (Set-Cookie) and security policy. Many production bugs are header bugs.

first_principles.problem: A CDN serves gzipped content to clients that didn't ask for it because the origin forgot Vary: Accept-Encoding.

analogy.title: Labels and instructions on a parcel
analogy.story: 'Fragile', 'this side up', 'deliver to reception' tell handlers what to do without opening it.
analogy.breaks: Parcel labels are rarely forged; X-Forwarded-For from clients can be.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No body re-sent; cache revalidated cheaply.

code.text:
GET /logo.png HTTP/1.1
If-None-Match: "abc123"

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: "abc123"
Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400

check.q: Why is Vary important for caches?
check.a: It tells caches which request headers change the response, so they store separate variants (e.g. gzip vs plain).

crucial-concept-idempotency-and-safety.core: A safe method doesn't change server state (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS). An idempotent method has the same effect whether executed once or many times (all safe methods, plus PUT and DELETE). POST and PATCH are neither by default. Because networks fail mid-request, clients and proxies retry, and only idempotent operations are safe to retry blindly. Make POSTs retry-safe with idempotency keys.

first_principles.problem: A payment POST times out, the client retries, and the customer is charged twice.
truths: Networks fail after the server acts.
Clients can't tell whether it succeeded.

analogy.title: A lift button
analogy.story: Pressing it five times still calls one lift (idempotent); ordering five pizzas by repeating the call isn't.
analogy.breaks: Pizzerias may ask 'is this a repeat?'; servers need the key to know.

code.text:
POST /v1/charges HTTP/1.1
Idempotency-Key: 7f3c2a1e-9b4d-4e1a-8c55-2f0e6b1d9a77
Content-Type: application/json

{"amount": 4999, "currency": "usd"}
# retry with same key → server returns original 201 response, no second charge

check.q: Is DELETE idempotent even though the second call returns 404?
check.a: Yes, idempotency concerns the server state effect (resource gone), not identical response codes.

the-tls-handshake-making-http-secure-htt.core: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. In TLS 1.3 the client sends ClientHello with supported ciphers, key shares and SNI (the hostname); the server replies with ServerHello, its key share, its certificate and a signature proving it holds the private key. Both derive session keys via ECDHE, and the client validates the certificate chain to a trusted CA and the hostname. That takes 1 round trip, or 0-RTT on resumption.

first_principles.problem: Users see certificate errors after a deploy because the server presents a cert missing the intermediate CA.
derivation: Use **SNI** for multiple hosts per IP.

analogy.title: Showing a notarised passport and agreeing a secret code
analogy.story: The passport (cert) is vouched for by an authority (CA), and both sides derive a code no eavesdropper can reconstruct.
analogy.breaks: Passports are checked visually; TLS checks cryptographic signatures and hostnames.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Missing level 1 would explain client errors.

code.text:
openssl s_client -connect shop.example.com:443 -servername shop.example.com -showcerts </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -E 's:|i:'
# 0 s:CN=shop.example.com  i:CN=R11
# 1 s:CN=R11               i:CN=ISRG Root X1

check.a: Session keys can't be recovered later even if the server's private key is stolen, because they came from ephemeral key exchange.

browser-security-headers-cors-and-conten.core: Browsers enforce the same-origin policy: scripts from one origin can't read responses from another. CORS lets servers relax this deliberately with Access-Control-Allow-Origin and preflight OPTIONS requests. Other headers harden pages: Content-Security-Policy limits script sources against XSS, HSTS forces HTTPS, X-Content-Type-Options stops MIME sniffing, and frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options prevents clickjacking.

first_principles.problem: A frontend on app.example.com can't call api.example.com, and a developer 'fixes' it with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * plus credentials.
truths: Servers must opt in to sharing.

analogy.title: Building security that only lets residents into flats
analogy.story: A resident can put a named guest on the list (CORS); house rules (CSP) forbid strangers' furniture (scripts).
analogy.breaks: Guests can be vetted in person; browsers only check headers.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only the app origin can call the API; XSS and clickjacking surface reduced.

code.text:
# API response
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Vary: Origin
# HTML response
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com; frame-ancestors 'none'
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

check.q: Why can't you use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials?
check.a: Browsers forbid it because it would let any site make authenticated requests and read the responses.
